Hermes Agent vs OpenCode is one of my favourite comparisons because the answer is “both, together”. OpenCode is a free, open-source coding agent with free models built in; Hermes is a free, always-on agent that runs your workflows. In my setup, OpenCode’s free models are the brain inside Hermes. Key takeaways

OpenCode: free coding agent with free models like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash.
Hermes: free always-on agent with memory, cron and messaging.

My free stack: OpenCode inside Hermes
This is how I run a lot of work for free: Hermes is the agent, and OpenCode provides a free brain such as DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. I’ve used this exact stack to analyse Search Console data and plan GEO content — see my GEO for websites guide. OpenCode is also a provider option inside Hermes (OpenCode Zen and OpenCode Go).
When to use OpenCode on its own

Quick coding jobs and prototypes.
Building apps from screenshots with vision models.
Testing new free models as they launch.
Coding when your paid model is rate limited.

When to use Hermes

Scheduled jobs and reports.
Tasks across your apps and messaging platforms.
Long-running work on a VPS.
Anything that benefits from memory and reusable skills.

Free models to try
OpenCode regularly offers free models — recently DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, GLM 5.3 Flash, Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and others. Free windows change, so keep a backup model ready in both tools.
How I set up the free stack
Install OpenCode and Hermes. In OpenCode, check which free models are available — recently DeepSeek V4.1 Flash has been a great choice. In Hermes, add OpenCode as a provider (OpenCode Zen or OpenCode Go) in hermes model, select the free model, and save it in its own profile. Now Hermes’ memory, skills and scheduling run on a free brain. When a free window closes, switch the profile to another free model.
Coding vs operating
The simplest way to think about it: OpenCode is where you build, Hermes is where things run. OpenCode is excellent for quick coding sessions, especially with vision models that can read screenshots. Hermes is where scheduled jobs, reports and messaging workflows live. Many of my automations start as an OpenCode session and end up as a Hermes skill.
What to watch out for
Free models can be rate limited or change without notice, so always keep a second free model ready in both tools. Review code before running it, especially if Hermes will run it on a schedule with access to your files or accounts. And keep approvals on in Hermes for anything that sends messages or deletes files.
Best choice by type of user

Beginners: start with Hermes Desktop and add OpenCode as a free model source.
Developers: start with OpenCode for coding, add Hermes for automation.
Agencies: use the pair to run client workflows on free models and keep costs near zero.
Creators: OpenCode to build small tools, Hermes to publish and report on a schedule.

Whichever you choose, start with one real job, keep approvals on for anything risky, and expand once it’s working reliably. The best agent is the one you actually use every day, and the fastest way to find it is to test it on your own work rather than reading feature lists.
Common mistakes
Expecting OpenCode to run scheduled jobs on its own is one; it’s a coding agent, not an always-on assistant. Another is leaving Hermes on a paid model for every routine job when a free OpenCode model would do. And a third is not keeping a backup free model — when a free window closes, your automations stop until you switch. Avoid those three and the free stack runs smoothly for months.
Get started this week: install OpenCode, pick a free model, add it to Hermes, and schedule one daily job.
The bottom line on Hermes Agent vs OpenCode
In Hermes Agent vs OpenCode, OpenCode is the free coder and free brain; Hermes is the free operator. Put them together and you have a powerful agent stack for nothing.
The free stack is the best way to learn agents without spending anything: OpenCode gives you free models and a fast coding agent, and Hermes turns those free models into an assistant that remembers you, runs jobs on a schedule and messages you the results. When you’re ready for more power, swap in a paid model for the hard jobs and keep the free one for everything else.

items.content:
Hermes Agent vs Hermes Desktop confuses a lot of people, so here’s the short answer: they’re the same agent. Hermes Agent is the open-source agent from Nous Research; Hermes Desktop is the official app for using it on Mac and Windows. The command line, the desktop app and your chat apps all talk to the same Hermes underneath. In the video below I show Hermes Desktop setting up local AI in one click. Here’s what each gives you.

Key takeaways

Hermes Desktop is the official app for Hermes Agent — same agent, same memory.
Desktop adds one-click plugins, connectors, local models and a setup chat.
The CLI is better for scripting, servers and the background gateway.
Use both — they stay in sync.

A guided setup chat on a free trial model — no API key needed.
A plugin catalogue with 600 reviewed plugins, installed in one click.
A Connectors page for apps like Notion and Linear, with multiple accounts.
One-click local models — Hermes picks the best model for your hardware.

Running on servers and VPSs.
Installing the background gateway service (hermes gateway install).

They stay in sync
Because the desktop app, the CLI, the dashboard and your messaging apps all use the same Hermes, your memory, skills, profiles and scheduled jobs are shared. I use Desktop for plugins and day-to-day chats, the CLI for my VPS, and Telegram on the go — and my automations show up everywhere.
Hermes Desktop alternatives
If you want a different interface on the same agent, there are free community options like Herald OS and Hermes3D, and my Agent OS runs Hermes alongside other agents. See my best Hermes Agent UI guide.

Start with Hermes Desktop. Since v0.22, a fresh install opens a guided setup chat that asks your name, preferences and which apps to connect, then suggests your first tasks — on a free trial model, so you don’t need an API key. Once you’re comfortable, install the CLI too, so you can run the background gateway and scheduled jobs.

Both. Use Hermes Desktop for browsing and installing plugins, managing connectors, watching Bot Screen and day-to-day chats. Use the CLI for servers, backups (hermes backup), updates, the gateway service and scripting. Because they share the same data, there’s no cost to using both.

Hermes Agent vs Pi coding agent comes down to what you’re coding. Pi coding agent is a lean terminal coding agent built around read, write, edit and bash, with subscription logins for ChatGPT, Claude and Copilot. Pi coding agent: lean, fast, transparent terminal coder.
Hermes: codes well and also runs, schedules and reports.

For pure coding sessions, Pi or a dedicated coder; for coding plus automation, Hermes.

A clean split: build in a coding agent (Pi, Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode), then hand the finished script to Hermes to run and monitor. That plays to each tool’s strengths.

Pi coding agent installs from npm and can sign in with subscriptions you already have, so you can be coding in minutes. Any agent that can run bash commands can also break things. Pi runs in your terminal, so review what it does. Hermes offers sandboxed terminal backends like Docker, which keep commands contained, and approvals for risky actions. Whichever you use, test on a copy of your project and keep backups.

You get a fast coder and a reliable operator.

Then whichever coding agent you use — Pi, Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode — can pick up where the last one left off, and Hermes can keep running the results reliably.

items.content:
Hermes Agent vs Pi is a clash of philosophies. Pi, by Mario Zechner, is a deliberately minimal open-source agent: four core tools and a short system prompt, with everything else added through extensions. Hermes is the opposite: a full-featured agent with memory, skills, 60+ tools, scheduling and 20+ messaging platforms out of the box. In the video below I explain why Hermes changed AI agents for me. Here’s how they compare.

Key takeaways

Pi: minimal by design — read, write, edit, bash, plus extensions.
Hermes: batteries included — memory, skills, cron, messaging, plugins.
Both are open source and free to run.
Pick Pi for control and simplicity, Hermes for out-of-the-box automation.

Two philosophies
Pi’s idea is that a small, transparent core is easier to understand, trust and extend: you start with four tools and add exactly what you need with TypeScript extensions. It’s popular with developers who want to know exactly what their agent is doing — and its components are used in other projects; Zechner has said OpenClaw uses them as its agent engine.
Hermes’ idea is that most people want an agent that works out of the box: memory that learns them, skills it writes itself, scheduled jobs, 20+ messaging platforms and a catalogue of 600 plugins. Since v0.22 you can even set it up through a chat with no API key.

When I need to build something — a dashboard, a tool, a site — Claude Code is the one I reach for. It’s not trying to be your always-on assistant; it’s trying to write excellent code.

How I use all three together

Claude Code builds the tools and automations.

Hermes runs them on a schedule and reports back.

OpenClaw handles quick personal tasks through chat.

An Agent OS puts them in one dashboard with shared memory.

You can even use your Claude subscription as Hermes’s brain through a plugin — check Anthropic’s terms first.

Which should you start with?

Start with Hermes if you want an agent that runs your business. Start with Claude Code if you mostly build software. Try OpenClaw if you want the simplest possible personal assistant. Most people end up with two or three of them.

Costs across the three

Hermes and OpenClaw are free and open source; you pay only for the models you use, and both can run on free or local models. Claude Code needs a Claude subscription or API usage. In practice, a sensible budget is one paid Claude plan for coding and free models for Hermes’ routine work, which keeps costs low while giving you the best tool for each job.

A workflow that uses all three

Here’s a real pattern. I ask Claude Code to build a small tool — say, a script that pulls my Search Console data and writes a summary. Hermes runs that script every Monday morning on my VPS and sends the summary to Telegram. During the week, when I need something quick — book a reminder, find a file, check a fact — I message OpenClaw or Hermes from my phone. Each agent does what it’s best at, and nothing falls through the cracks.

Common mistakes when choosing

The most common mistake is expecting one agent to do everything. A coding agent left running as a personal assistant is overkill and expensive; a personal assistant asked to refactor a large codebase will struggle. The second mistake is ignoring safety: whichever agents you use, keep approvals on for anything that sends, buys or deletes, and don’t expose them to the public internet.

Best choice by type of user

Business owners: start with Hermes, add Claude Code when you need a custom tool built.

Developers: start with Claude Code, add Hermes to run and monitor what you build.

Personal users: OpenClaw or Hermes for everyday assistance through chat apps.

Whichever you choose, start with one real job, keep approvals on for anything risky, and expand once it’s working reliably. The best agent is the one you actually use every day, and the fastest way to find it is to test it on your own work rather than reading feature lists.

Getting started with all three

Install Hermes first and connect Telegram, so you have an always-on agent. Add Claude Code when you need to build something. Try OpenClaw if you want a second personal assistant with a different feel. Within a week you’ll know which jobs belong to which agent, and an Agent OS can bring them together on one screen.

The bottom line

In Hermes Agent vs OpenClaw vs Claude Code, there’s no single winner: Hermes runs, OpenClaw assists and Claude Code builds. Use each for its job.

One last thought: these tools are improving every month. Hermes added keyless setup, connectors and one-click local models in v0.22; Claude Code keeps getting stronger with each Claude release; and OpenClaw has a foundation and OpenAI’s support behind it. Rather than betting on one winner, build your workflows as skills and scripts you own, so you can move them between agents as the landscape changes.
